title: Corrective Action Should Be Instigated Quickly: the Memo That Was Ignored, and the Phrase That Followed
participants: Continental Illinois National Bank and Trust Company
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The growth was bought wholesale. Continental competed aggressively for oil and gas loans "amid the United States' drive for energy independence and funded that expansion with large-scale borrowing from money markets", acquiring by 1981 "a large amount of oil and gas loans from Penn Square Bank", an Oklahoma bank the essay describes as having "a freewheeling culture". A Penn Square client is quoted: "I could hardly believe it — they loaned me $2.5 million hardly asking any questions and then sold the loan to Continental."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was in the funding mix and it was partly statutory: Illinois law forbade branch banking, so the bank "had little ability to scale up funding from stable retail deposits", and at the time of its rescue "insured deposits comprised only about 15 percent of Continental's total liabilities." A bank funded by large uninsured creditors is a bank that can be left in a morning.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The warning existed, in writing, inside the bank, and this node exists because of it. An employee in Continental's oil and gas division "warned in an internal memo that 'potential credit problems could be going unnoticed' in those loans, and recommended that 'corrective action should be instigated quickly.' Her warnings, largely ignored, proved prescient when Penn Square failed in 1982". The essay extends the failure outward: "Neither Continental's own internal control system nor federal regulators' supervisory efforts fully appreciated the extent of these problems."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was a guarantee no depositor had paid for. The run began around 7 May 1984 and took about 30 percent of the bank's funding in ten days, "generally electronic and spearheaded by depositors with large uninsured deposits and other bank creditors". It stopped on 17 May when the FDIC, Federal Reserve and OCC announced an assistance programme whose "most important element was the FDIC's announcement that it would guarantee of all of the bank's creditors", with a $2 billion FDIC loan and a Federal Reserve statement that it was "prepared to meet any extraordinary liquidity requirements".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The resolution was ownership rather than an inquiry: when the run resumed the FDIC took "80 percent ownership in Continental's holding company" and assumed its Federal Reserve loan. The losses were distributed unevenly and the essay records it: "its shareholders lost their investments in the bank and its management was fired", while uninsured creditors were made whole, and "The FDIC ultimately estimated its loss was about $1.1 billion, equal to about 3 percent of Continental's assets at the time of its intervention."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Deposit insurance designed for small depositors, applied to a bank whose liabilities were overwhelmingly uninsured and wholesale, under a state branching prohibition that made retail funding impossible.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The doctrine itself: "The phrase 'too big to fail' became commonly used for the first time after Continental's crisis", and with it the expectation that the creditors of a sufficiently large bank are covered whether or not the insurance says so.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Wholesale funding bought loan growth; loan growth required more wholesale funding; the uninsured creditors who supplied it could leave electronically in a morning, which is precisely why they had to be guaranteed when they tried to.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Continental Illinois was the first bank bailout, in which Washington simply handed public money to a reckless bank and nobody suffered.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The distribution of loss is on the record and it is not "nobody". Continental's "shareholders lost their investments in the bank and its management was fired", and the FDIC estimated its own loss at about $1.1 billion. What was rescued was the creditor class: the FDIC guaranteed all of the bank's creditors, including the large uninsured depositors whose electronic withdrawals had caused the run. That is the precise thing worth naming, and it is more specific than "bailout" — it is a guarantee extended to people who had not bought one, in a bank whose insured deposits were only about 15 percent of its liabilities. The counter-reading, that regulators acted on a whim, also fails: the essay records the decision following "vigorous internal debate about a range of possible options".
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Oil and gas loans purchased in volume from Penn Square Bank by 1981. An internal memo from Continental's own oil and gas division warning that "potential credit problems could be going unnoticed" and that "corrective action should be instigated quickly", largely ignored, before Penn Square failed in 1982. Neither the bank's internal controls nor federal supervision appreciating the extent of the problem. Insured deposits at about 15 percent of total liabilities. A run from about 7 May 1984 taking roughly 30 percent of funding in ten days, led by large uninsured depositors and other creditors. An assistance programme announced on 17 May guaranteeing all of the bank's creditors, with a $2 billion FDIC loan and a Federal Reserve commitment on liquidity. A second run, then 80 percent FDIC ownership of the holding company. Shareholders wiped out, management fired, and an FDIC loss of about $1.1 billion — and a phrase that entered common use for the first time.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Continental Illinois: A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail, May 1984" (published 15 May 2023)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from federalreservehistory.org. On the origin of the phrase: the essay is subtitled "A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail" and records that "The phrase 'too big to fail' became commonly used for the first time after Continental's crisis", and that the episode "ignited a national debate that continues to this day over whether large financial institutions enjoy undue privileges because regulators consider them too big to fail." THE WARNING THAT WAS IGNORED, which is the heart of this node: as Continental's purchases of oil and gas loans from Penn Square Bank accumulated, "an employee in Continental's oil and gas division warned in an internal memo that 'potential credit problems could be going unnoticed' in those loans, and recommended that 'corrective action should be instigated quickly.' Her warnings, largely ignored, proved prescient when Penn Square failed in 1982". The essay adds: "Neither Continental's own internal control system nor federal regulators' supervisory efforts fully appreciated the extent of these problems." On the funding structure: Illinois law forbade branch banking, so the bank "had little ability to scale up funding from stable retail deposits", and "At the time of its rescue, insured deposits comprised only about 15 percent of Continental's total liabilities." On the run: "A large-scale run by depositors on Continental began around May 7, 1984 ... Over the next ten days, the bank lost about 30 percent of its funding. The run was generally electronic and spearheaded by depositors with large uninsured deposits and other bank creditors." On the rescue: it stopped on 17 May when the FDIC, Federal Reserve and OCC announced a temporary assistance program, of which "The most important element was the FDIC's announcement that it would guarantee of all of the bank's creditors" (the grammatical slip is the essay's); the FDIC also lent $2 billion, and the Federal Reserve announced it "is prepared to meet any extraordinary liquidity requirements". When the run resumed, the FDIC took "80 percent ownership in Continental's holding company". On who bore the loss: "its shareholders lost their investments in the bank and its management was fired", and "The FDIC ultimately estimated its loss was about $1.1 billion, equal to about 3 percent of Continental's assets at the time of its intervention."
